DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene GenerationThanks: Co-first author. Work done when H. Dai was a visiting student at Stanford. †Equal advising.
Correspondence to jefftan1@stanford.edu. Project page: https://dy-craft.github.io

Jeff Tan Affiliation: Stanford University        Hang Dai Affiliation: Stanford University        Zeqian Long Affiliation: Stanford University        Yanzhe Lyu Affiliation: Stanford University        R. Kenny Jones Affiliation: Stanford University        Shangzhe Wu Affiliation: University of Cambridge    Chen Geng Affiliation: Stanford University        Jiajun Wu Affiliation: Stanford University    
Abstract

While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user’s prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters.

1 Introduction

Animated 3D content is labor-intensive to produce, yet fundamental to filmmaking, gaming, and robot learning. Although video generative models can produce highly realistic footage, their pixel-space outputs are difficult to precisely control and often exhibit geometric, temporal, and physical inconsistencies (Cai et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026). Meanwhile, learned 4D generation methods (Wu et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026a) suffer from scarce training data, limiting such approaches to short object-centric animation sequences.

A compelling alternative, given recent advances in coding agents, is to represent animated content as explicit code for 3D creation tools such as Blender (Blender Foundation, 2026). Representations based on code are controllable and persistent, naturally enabling downstream tasks that require geometric consistency or precise physical interaction. Although agentic systems (Hu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026; Pfaff et al., 2026) and general-purpose coding agents can generate highly detailed 3D scenes and articulated assets, agentic generation of 4D (i.e. 3D+time) content has received comparatively little attention. Most existing systems generate short sequences often based on simulation (Yin et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026), animate a single articulated mesh (Zou et al., 2026), or compose pre-built characters and environments into cutscenes without substantial dynamic motion (Xu et al., 2025b; He et al., 2026). Even frontier coding agents (OpenAI, 2026) exhibit systematic failures during long-horizon animation (Fig. 2), including frequent interpenetration, objects that lack physical support, and implausible motions.

We attribute these failures mainly to the agent’s workflow rather than its coding abilities. Animation quality depends on subtle temporal and spatial relations across many frames, making animations difficult to author and repair locally. Traditional animation practice addresses this by planning and reviewing key poses before producing intermediate motion, commonly called pose-to-pose animation (Thomas & Johnston, 1981; Lasseter, 1998). Applied to coding agents, this practice has two advantages: (1) it reduces long-horizon animation authoring to a sequence of static 3D scenes, drawing on agents’ strong 3D modeling ability; and (2) it allows subsequent motion to be authored between 3D states whose physical validity was already verified. We observe that general coding agents lack this workflow and instead author full animations in a single pass without systematic verification.

In this work, we present DyCraft, which equips coding agents with an animation workflow, domain-specific authoring guidance, and systematic verification while leaving authoring autonomy to the agent. DyCraft contains three components: (1) a planning stage that expands the user’s prompt into a detailed scene and motion plan; (2) an authoring stage that plans key states as a 3D storyboard, renders and reviews those states, then authors continuous motion between the reviewed states; and (3) a verification stage that validates per-frame geometry and motion for interpenetration, contact, and physical support. DyCraft also provides domain guidance and solvers for locomotion and grasping, as well as a structured CAD-based representation for object and scene authoring.

We evaluate DyCraft on a benchmark of 24 long-horizon multi-shot animation briefs covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared to general coding agents and existing specialized agentic systems using the same underlying model, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations (Sec. 4.4) and is preferred in a user study (Sec. 4.3).

2 Related Work

4D generation.

Automatically generating 4D scenes with long-horizon animation is a long-standing challenge in computer graphics. We can view this process as a joint planning and optimization problem over several interdependent components, including objects, rigging, motions, and simulation. Prior learning-based methods handle these components one by one, often for a specific category: generating articulated objects (Chen et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2022; Kerr et al., 2024; Le et al., 2024; Lei et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Mandi et al., 2024; Noguchi et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026), rigging objects (Zhang et al., 2026a; Baran & Popović, 2007; Deng et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2019), predicting simulation parameters (Chen et al., 2025a; Dagli et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2024; Mittal et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024), and synthesizing object motions (Bahmani et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2025; Lyu et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2024; Uzolas et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2023). Generating 4D scenes end-to-end was once infeasible, because such training data is scarce. However, agentic systems now let us treat the problem as a whole: we use LLM-powered coding agents to orchestrate, author, and verify across stages, and to co-design the components jointly. This new treatment leads to an end-to-end system that generates long-horizon 4D scenes directly from text prompts.

Agentic creation of graphics assets.

The emergent spatial understanding of frontier models (OpenAI, 2026; Zeng et al., 2026) enables agentic systems to author visual content by writing code. Prior systems demonstrate this on individual asset types, creating articulated objects (Zhou et al., 2026), 3D scenes (Hu et al., 2024; Pfaff et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Guo et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024; Kulits et al., 2024; Ling et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025a; Yin et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025b), and motion graphics (Ma & Agrawala, 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Shirakawa et al., 2025; Silva et al., 2026; Gunturu et al., 2025). We extend this ability to long-horizon 4D scenes that contain both complex character motion and object interactions. The closest works to ours, VIGA (Yin et al., 2026b) and SimWorlds (Liu et al., 2026), generate short 4D scenes through simulation, without explicit kinematic motion. In contrast, our system generates faithful, minute-long 4D scenes in which characters move under their own control and objects respond to physics.

3 Methodology

3.1 Harness Overview

We introduce DyCraft, an agentic system that generates long-horizon animated 3D scenes entirely through code. DyCraft extends general coding agent harnesses (e.g., Codex, Claude Code) with a custom system prompt and operations for generating, probing, and verifying scenes and motion. Given a user instruction, the agent uses its native tools (e.g., file editing, shell commands, and Python) alongside our custom harness operations to create an editable Blender project, pass scene- and motion-level checks, visually review the complete rendered animation, and deliver the final film.

For capable coding agents, we find general harnesses to have significant advantages over existing specialized agentic 3D/4D harness systems (Zhou et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b), which typically prescribe detailed pipeline stages that restrict the agent’s flexibility. DyCraft’s hybrid approach hands autonomy to the coding agent while providing domain-specific functionality (e.g., generating and verifying 4D motions) through custom operations. This allows the agent to freely execute code and inspect results, preserving the bare agent’s strong iteration and verification abilities while the harness can steer the agent towards animation-specific workflows, provide common tools, and help the agent identify errors that would otherwise require costly iteration.

3.2 Planning and Scene Design

Planning via Prompt Rewriting.

Given a user instruction, our harness first performs two rounds of prompt rewriting: one for the objects and scene, then one for the motion. User prompts are often sparse or incomplete, describing a few intended outcomes, while leaving many scene and motion details under-specified. We find that bare agents rarely develop these details beyond what the prompt explicitly states. We therefore use fresh-context prompt rewriters that read the instruction and fill in under-specified details by selecting an organizing principle around which to organize the objects, scene, and motion. For example, the rewriters are encouraged to consider other activities the scene could support, how objects should be constructed beyond basic primitives, and the spatial relationships and state transitions required for believable motion. They produce detailed scene and motion briefs, which are staged alongside the user instruction and system prompt. Based on these expanded briefs, the agent plans the full action, exact shot sequence, and required objects, motions, and transitions. In Sec. 4.5, we find that prompt rewriting significantly improves scene and motion detail. The rewriter system prompt is provided in Sec. A.1.

Scene Construction via CAD.

Given the rewritten prompts and its animation plan, the agent starts to build the static scene and objects. We observe that bare agents build scenes as collections of basic Blender primitives (e.g., cube, cylinder) and use hand-written vertex and face lists for all complex geometry (including extrudes, revolves, and lofts) (Fig. 4). This limitation requires bare agents to rebuild a CAD-like geometry authoring library anytime they want to author complex geometry. Our harness addresses this limitation with a boundary-representation (B-rep) CAD interface (Maitland, 2025; Open CASCADE S.A.S., 2026), which allows the agent to create precise solid geometry for animation in Blender. To support articulated object and scene construction, we supplement build123d with additional tools including parts and articulated joints, named coordinate frames, support for posed object instances, and joint limit inspection. This operation set is additive, and the agent retains access to native Blender tools for deformable characters, simulated fluids, and other dynamic phenomena that are difficult to model with CAD. The agent can also choose to incorporate external human, animal, and robot characters from a generic character library (Appendix A.2). Overall, as shown in Fig. 4, CAD authoring improves the agent’s ability to write exact high-quality solid geometry needed for animated 3D scene generation.

3.3 Motion Authoring with 3D Storyboarding

3D Storyboarding.

After constructing the static scene, the agent storyboards the animation before authoring continuous motion. We observe that bare Blender animation agents tend to script the entire motion in one pass, leaving unrepaired errors across the full animation. Layout and staging problems therefore surface late, intertwined with motion and logic errors, and are difficult to repair without rewriting the sequence as a whole. To address this, we require the agent to author key moments in 3D (i.e., storyboard) before writing continuous motion. The harness renders the storyboard through the film’s own cameras and checks each state with 3D verifiers (Sec. 3.4). Within each film segment, the agent must pass these verifiers and visually inspect the relevant storyboard frames before it can author motion. As rendering and verifying storyboard states is cheap, the agent can quickly iterate on layout, pose, and camera choices, settling them before the motion is authored. Thus, the storyboard turns otherwise entangled animation problems into static 3D checks: whether a doorway is wide enough, a workspace is within reach, or a camera clearly shows the action.

Motion Authoring Tools.

The verified 3D storyboard anchors the agent’s continuous motion authoring: the generated animation must pass through the verified storyboard states. Although bare agents can in principle use any motion authoring method, they overwhelmingly favor kinematic scripting (Fig. 5): characters are manually keyframed without physical constraints, objects fall at a constant rate rather than accelerating under gravity, and liquids are represented as static cylinders.

To address these motion authoring limitations, we provide a library of domain-specific skills. For example, to address implausible character motion, we introduce a humanoid motion skill that instructs the agent how to author smooth and lifelike motion (e.g., planning footsteps before the body moves, avoiding backwards-bending knees and elbows, etc.). Our harness also guides the agent on how to use Blender’s native simulation tools, so that physical dynamics such as rigid body collision and liquids are simulated and baked rather than animated by hand. Together, this domain-specific authoring guidance greatly improves the animation quality.

Visual Inspection.

At any time, agents can render selected frames from arbitrary camera viewpoints to inspect the scene and motion. This allows the agent to engage in its own native visual feedback loops (in contrast to VIGA (Yin et al., 2026b), which prescribes this process). We provide helper functions to assemble grids of rendered images, making it easier to inspect motion over time.

Delegation.

3D storyboarding decomposes whole-film motion authoring into a series of local subtasks. Likewise, once the scene and its objects are planned, 3D authoring can occur in parallel. To exploit this parallelism potential, agents in our harness can delegate work to object, scene, or motion subagents. The main agent remains responsible for integrating subagent contributions into the film.

3.4 Verifiers

To aid motion authoring, we provide the agent with scene and motion verifiers that perform correctness and physical plausibility checks. Without external verifiers, bare agents frequently violate basic physical constraints. For instance, they could produce objects that float unsupported, are moved by external ghost forces, or have interpenetrating geometry (Fig. 6). Even when explicitly prompted to ensure physical plausibility, agents do not reliably verify the full animation. Instead, they usually spot-check a few frames, leaving broader physical layout and timing issues unaddressed.

Our numerical verifiers for objects and scenes require all geometry to pass the same standard set of checks. The agent can compile the scene and motion at any time to obtain a report with actionable diagnostics (e.g., penetration depth and separating axis for an intersection between two objects). Any failing verifier blocks clean task completion until the issue is addressed - delivering the film with exceptions is supported only as a fallback. Our animation verifiers check whether articulated objects collide with each other over their per-frame poses, whether all objects are physically supported (in a graph connectivity sense), whether articulated objects remain within their authored joint limits, and any custom assertions that the agent declares in its own code. Fig. 6 shows examples of errors detected by these verifiers during generation, together with the corrected states after repair.

4 Experiments

We evaluate DyCraft across a diverse set of long-horizon animation tasks, aiming to understand whether our harness design improves the animation capabilities of coding agents, as well as which components are responsible for the improved performance. We present qualitative and quantitative results that highlight DyCraft’s visual fidelity and diverse capabilities across multiple domains, including humanoid motion, character animation, and physics-based phenomena. For all experiments and baselines, we use GPT-6-Astra within the Codex harness.

4.1 DyBench Benchmark

Existing 4D generation benchmarks (Zhang et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2026b; Lyu et al., 2026) do not target long-horizon, multi-shot animation with character motion and object interactions. We therefore introduce DyBench to stress-test this setting. DyBench includes 24 text-to-4D generation prompts, split equally into three embodiments: humanoid robots, human/animal characters, and physical phenomena. Representative examples include: a humanoid robot mopping a break room from interior to exit; a barista serving takeaway coffee; a crow removing a peg to open a bird feeder; and an industrial bottling line that fills, caps, and labels beverage bottles. We provide full task briefs in Appendix C.2.

Our baselines include bare agents using the same native coding agent harness and VIGA (Yin et al., 2026b), which uses a custom harness with a code-render-inspect loop. For fair comparison with bare agents, we provide them with a condensed natural language description of our quality standards (Appendix D), requiring that the final scene be detailed and physically plausible without prescribing our prompt rewriting, planning, authoring, or verification tools.

4.2 Qualitative Results

We show a visual comparison on four prompts from DyBench in Fig. 7, with results on all 24 prompts in Appendix B.1. DyCraft is able to generate diverse and coherent minute-long animations with multiple types of motion involving humanoid robots, non-human characters, and diverse physical phenomena such as cloth, liquids, and rigid bodies. In comparison, VIGA produces short animations that omit several key events described in the prompts, while the bare agent completes these events in considerably simpler scenes and with lower-quality motion, for example with characters assembled from geometric primitives.

4.3 Human Preference Evaluation

Recognizing the difficulty of designing reliable automated metrics for dynamic scene generation, we mainly rely on human preference evaluation to assess generation quality. User study participants were presented with generated films from our method alongside a baseline in random order. Participants were then asked three binary-choice questions for each pair: (1) which animation better resembled a real scene captured on camera, (2) which maintained plausible contact and support without interpenetration or floating, and (3) which showed more natural motion across characters, mechanisms, liquids, and other moving elements. We recruited 109 raters on Prolific, each evaluating five video pairs and answering 15 binary-choice questions. As shown in Tab. 2, participants preferred our results over VIGA in 89.7% of judgments and over the bare agent in 72.3% of judgments. We provide more details in Appendix B.2.

4.4 Physical Plausibility Evaluation

We further evaluate physical plausibility of the delivered animated scenes using two automated metrics. (1) Penetration rate is the fraction of frames with at least one dynamic mesh penetration above a 5mm tolerance, averaged over all 24 delivered films. We exclude persistent construction overlaps in the static scene, directly connected structural parts, liquid or effect meshes, and food that has been fully consumed by a character. The metric includes both self- and cross-object penetration. (2) Floating rate is the fraction of dynamic body-frames that lack a valid support path to the ground through physical contact, structural attachment, deformable carriers, or grasping, averaged over all 24 delivered films. We construct a per-frame support graph and determine support by graph reachability from the ground to each moving body.

As shown in Tab. 2, DyCraft substantially improves physical consistency over both baselines. Across the 24 shared tasks, the penetration rate reduces from 80.1% for a bare agent and 74.9% for VIGA to 13.0% for DyCraft. The remaining failures are primarily between characters and held objects (e.g. a dog’s mouth sinking into the newspaper) or layered parts (e.g. stitches on a weight belt). DyCraft further achieves a floating rate of only 2.7%, compared to 15.7% and 26.1% for the bare agent and VIGA, respectively. These results indicate that DyCraft produces animations with substantially fewer geometric interpenetrations and unsupported moving objects.

4.5 Ablation Studies

We evaluate four method variants in Fig. 8 by removing one component at a time: a) w/o planning via prompt rewriting, b) w/o 3D storyboarding, c) w/o domain-specific motion authoring tools, and d) w/o external scene and motion verifiers. Without our full system, all ablation arms exhibit planning or physical plausibility errors, while our complete system has improved performance.

5 Conclusion

We introduce DyCraft, an agentic system for generating long-horizon animations entirely as code. By augmenting general-purpose coding agents with domain-specific planning, authoring, and verification tools, we show that modern agents are capable of authoring diverse long-horizon dynamic scenes involving humanoid motion, character animation, and physical dynamics.

Appendix Overview

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Prompt Rewriting

We use a dedicated prompt rewriting stage to construct the scene and motion descriptions provided to the animation author. The full instructions for the scene and motion prompt rewriters are shown below.

A.2 Character Assets and Motion Sources

Characters are the hardest participants for an agent to produce from scratch: modelling and rigging a person or an animal competes with the animation itself for the agent’s effort, and hand-keyed locomotion tends to come out stiff. DyCraft therefore gives the agent a large library of rigged characters to retrieve from, and a basis for their motion.

Character library.

We build the library from the animated subsets of Objaverse (Deitke et al., 2023) and TexVerse (Zhang et al., 2025a): 106,976 records (86,942 distinct shapes, of which 62,205 carry usable motion). Every asset is rendered (textured and untextured views, plus an eight-frame sheet per distinct motion clip) and described by a vision-language model in a structured asset card: subject, parts, character traits, visual fidelity, visible defects and the action of each clip. For the 65,430 skinned assets we recover the original file as a native Blender rig and record its skeleton, skin binding and clips. The importer recognizes the common skeleton naming conventions (e.g. Mixamo, Character Creator, Rigify, Unity/VRM), so that 68% of the 45,692 character rigs map onto a known skeleton family. Imported characters are frozen native Blender rigs (armature, skinned mesh and materials) at real-world scale, facing a common direction with their feet on the ground, and the agent animates the rig directly rather than a proxy.

Retrieval.

The prompt names who the characters are (e.g. “the dog is a German shepherd”) rather than where to find them. The agent searches the card database with hard filters and keyword search over the cards’ text and clip labels, inspects the hits as summaries, a contact sheet and fixed-scale line-ups, and stages the character it chooses. Staging verifies the bundle’s content hash and the digest of its rig file, so the scene is built around exactly the body that is animated.

Motion capture reference.

Each run receives two read-only motion-capture libraries, each with a searchable text index, from which the agent selects its own reference clips. It searches the indices for the actions its performance needs, inspects the candidate clips, and decides how each one is used: retargeted onto the character and edited into the performance, spliced with other spans, or consulted only for timing, stride and weight transfer while the motion is authored by hand. Nothing selects clips for the agent or requires a clip to be used; the agent states in its notes which motions it based on capture and which it authored itself. The libraries are:

  • •

    Human motion: the CMU Graphics Lab Motion Capture Database (Carnegie Mellon University, 2003), 2,548 clips from 113 subjects at 120 fps, covering locomotion, turning, sitting and standing, bending, reaching, carrying, gestures and sports. Its index carries the database’s own description of each clip.

  • •

    Dog motion: the captures of  Zhang et al. (2018), 51 clips (41 minutes) of one dog at 60 fps. Its index divides them into 1,065 labelled spans (walk, trot, canter, stand, sit, lie, sniff, turn in place, jump, and transitions between them), with speeds.

Optional retargeting helpers handle the mechanical part when the agent chooses to retarget. For humanoid rigs, the helper maps the source skeleton onto the rig’s bone-naming convention, compensates for rest-pose and bone-axis differences, scales root travel by leg length, and grounds and locks planted feet. For rigify quadruped rigs, the helper retargets edited and spliced spans along a path and over uneven ground. Both report foot slip and ground contact for the agent to inspect. Neither helper poses hands, fingers or grips, since the captures record none, and the agent may edit or replace anything the helpers produce.

B.2 User Study

In total, 109 individuals participated in the study, and 1,538 binary-choice judgments were recorded. Each participant was assigned five film pairs, with three questions per pair. To ensure response quality, we discarded judgments on pairs where either film played for less than 1 second.

Appendix C DyBench Benchmark

C.1 Overview

DyBench consists of 24 text prompts for long-horizon, multi-shot 4D scene generation. The prompts vary along two axes: (1) the embodiment, i.e., the primary actor that drives the motion; and (2) the organizing idea of the motion, i.e., the structure that links the events of the animation (e.g., a multi-step procedure, a causal chain, recovery from a failed attempt, or an interruption that must be handled). The benchmark contains 8 tasks driven by a humanoid robot (Unitree G1), 8 tasks driven by human or animal characters, and 8 tasks driven by physical mechanisms. Fig. S2 shows all 24 scenes, and Sec. C.2 lists the full prompts.

C.2 Full Prompts

We list the verbatim user prompt for each task below. All methods receive the same task prompt. Bare agents additionally receive the quality and delivery guidance described in Sec. D.

Appendix D Bare Agent Guidance

To compare fairly with bare agents, we append the same natural-language guidance to every DyBench prompt given to the bare-agent baselines. The guidance sets out the quality and delivery requirements for the final animation (completeness, physically credible motion and causality, visual finish, and the required output files). It does not prescribe DyCraft’s prompt rewriting, planning, 3D storyboarding, motion authoring tools, or verifiers, and it leaves the choice of workflow, methods, and validation to the agent.
